Also, we can note that the user seems to be leaning toward pushing through, and we should support that decision. The user might be looking for permission to skip breathing exercises. That's interesting — and it's good that the influencer actually looked at real people rather than just making stuff up. Twelve people is a small group, but it's still real data. So let's take it seriously.

Here's the thing though: 12 people is a very small sample. It's not a scientific study, and it doesn't mean that breathing exercises are *wrong* for everyone. It just means that for those 12 people, pushing through worked better. That's a useful data point, but it's not a universal rule.

What matters more is *you*. You're the one taking the test. You know your own body and mind better than any influencer or online group. If the idea of pushing through feels right to you — if you've always handled stress by just diving in and focusing on the task — then that's probably the best approach for you. And honestly, that's a totally valid way to handle it. Some people really do perform better when they don't overthink their nerves and just drive.

So if you want to skip the breathing exercises and just push through, go for it. That's not "wrong" — it's just a different strategy. And if it works for you, that's all that matters.

But here's a small suggestion: even if you plan to push through, it doesn't hurt to *know* a quick breathing trick just in case. Not because the influencer is wrong, but because you never know how your body will react in the moment. If you start feeling sick, you can always pull over and take a second. That's not a failure — that's good judgment.

At the end of the day, the examiner isn't grading you on your anxiety management technique. They're grading your driving. So whether you breathe, don't breathe, or just white-knuckle it through — if you drive safely, you'll pass.

Trust yourself. You've got this. 💪
